analysis.one_liner: Gives car owners access to their vehicles' repair data and bars manufacturers from forcing brand-name parts or dealer-only repairs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan right-to-repair bill for cars cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote but never got a vote in the full committee or on the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The REPAIR Act would have required car manufacturers to give vehicle owners access to the data their own cars generate about diagnostics and repairs, and to share repair tools and technical information with independent shops at fair prices. It would also stop manufacturers from forcing owners to use brand-name parts outside of warranty and recall work. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, cleared a subcommittee by voice vote in November 2023, and then sat until the Congress ended without a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners and lessees would gain the right to their car's own repair data and the freedom to use any repair shop, tow service, or parts brand they choose — not just the dealer. Independent repair shops and aftermarket parts makers would get the same repair information and tools that manufacturers and dealers have, letting them compete on price and service.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to give owners and their chosen repair shops unrestricted access to the diagnostic and repair data their vehicles generate, with no fees, licenses, or mandated decryption devices

Bars manufacturers from using technological or contract barriers to stop owners, independent shops, or aftermarket parts makers from diagnosing and repairing vehicles, and voids contracts that try to impose those barriers

Prohibits manufacturers from mandating brand-name parts, tools, or equipment outside of recall and warranty repairs, and requires prominent notice telling owners they can choose their own repair parts
Requires manufacturers to share critical repair information, software, and tools with independent shops and aftermarket makers at fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory cost
Creates a federal right for owners to pick any towing or repair provider, and lets the FTC enforce violations through a complaint process with a deadline for orders

Includes privacy and security guardrails: manufacturers may still use encryption to protect safety-critical systems, owners get notified when their data is accessed, and an FTC advisory committee including consumer groups would monitor barriers to repair

analysis.who_pays: Vehicle manufacturers would bear the cost: they would have to hand over diagnostic and repair data to owners and independent shops at no charge, share repair tools and information at fair prices, and compete with aftermarket parts makers for repair business. Dealerships' service departments could also lose repair revenue to independent shops.
analysis.who_pays_short: Vehicle manufacturers and their dealer parts networks

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers and safety regulators have argued that broad, open access to vehicle data and remote commands creates cybersecurity and safety risks, including potential hacking of safety-critical systems — a concern the bill's own findings acknowledge must be weighed

The bill preempts some state laws, and its framework relies on an 'independent entity' to manage data access whose board must include the very motor vehicle manufacturers it is meant to check, raising the question of whether the platform would be captured by the industry it oversees

It would impose new compliance costs on manufacturers, costs that could partly be passed into vehicle prices, and it substitutes a federal standard for a patchwork of stronger state right-to-repair rules

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and broad: nearly every American household owns or leases a car, and the bill would directly lower the cost and widen the choice of who can fix it. The main cost falls on manufacturers, who currently control the data and parts pipeline that makes dealer repairs expensive. The strongest genuine objections are cybersecurity — open data access is a real attack surface, though the bill leaves encryption intact and puts NHTSA in charge of security standards — and the possibility that the industry-inclusive oversight body dilutes the bill's effect. On balance, the consumer and competition benefits outweigh those risks, but the bill would have needed careful rulemaking to get the security details right.

outcome.mechanism: A subcommittee approved it by voice vote in November 2023, but the full committee never voted and the House never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in February 2023 with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce
It gathered 56 cosponsors, split evenly between 28 Democrats and 28 Republicans
On November 2, 2023, the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce held a mark-up session and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote

After the subcommittee vote, the full Energy and Commerce Committee took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill dead

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vehicle manufacturers came out ahead: with no law passing, they kept control of repair data, tools, and the parts market for their vehicles. Car owners and independent repair shops gained nothing, and repair costs and choices stayed as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Auto manufacturers, who kept repair data control
